hero.caption:
Page 180 From De volkomen beschryvinge der voortreffelijcke reyzen van de deurluchtige reysiger Pietro della Valle, edelman van Romen, in veel voorname gewesten des Werelts gedaan, vol.2.
📘 English Translation of Page 180:
The Adventurous Journeys  
He reported that, after the enemy had launched their attack on the frontier, these tribes—living along the borders of the Persian realm and in the service of the Turks—showed themselves to be enemies of the Persians. By nature inclined to pillaging and looting, they carried out daily heavy and fierce raids into the borderlands of Persia, seizing everything they could lay hands on. But sometimes, when they stumbled, like beasts, their fate was disastrous.
A Gift of Severed Heads to the King
Two others joined forces to jointly present another gift. The larger portion of this gift came from Hussein Khan, a commander of a province situated near the borders of Baghdad. The smaller portion belonged to Kasuin Sultan, governor of the city under the aforementioned Khan and commander of certain units also stationed near the borders of Baghdad. He was traveling when he came from Isfahan, and it was said that he encountered some of his soldiers along the way.
Hussein Khan contributed six hundred heads of Turks, which he had captured; and the Sultan, who had fewer troops under his command, sent sixty heads. These two commanders, having gathered their forces, engaged in a swift and fierce battle, sacrificing these enemies to their wrath. The heads came from regions that were under Persian control. A place called Chieruk was plundered and devastated, and the Pasha of that region—named Gaifk Pasha—had ordered an attack on his enemies.
The head of this Pasha, along with the heads of two other prominent Tartars, who had wintered in that region with their troops, were wrapped in silk cloths to distinguish them from all the other heads, which were displayed bare and mounted on spears. Such a gift of enemy heads, as was shown to the King, is a very old custom, according to the account of Strabo.

The horse of the slain Pasha was entirely adorned with gold and silver, following the custom of the Turks, and was included among all these victims. Likewise, the commander whom the Pasha had ordered to attack stood out above all others in the gift, and to be considered especially important, he was decorated beyond his usual silver ornaments—something the wealthy and noble Pasha had provided. Also included were six living prisoners, who had iron collars around their necks and, being men of state, had previously held positions of authority.
